It says that customs and ways of life should be understood in their own context instead of being judged by the standards of your own culture. At the same time, people argue about whether there are values that apply to everyone, such as human rights.
wichtigste: Methodological cultural relativism aims to understand customs in their own context.
The opposite idea is called ethnocentrism, which means measuring other cultures against your own.
Ethical cultural relativism denies that there are moral standards valid for everyone.
Franz Boas, Ruth Benedict and Melville Herskovits shaped the idea in the USA.
Ruth Benedict's book “Patterns of Culture” from 1934 made the idea well known.
In 1947 the American Anthropological Association warned against making the values of one culture the standard for all.
Critics believe that radical cultural relativism could excuse human rights abuses.

abschnitte.text: Every culture has its own customs, rules and ideas about what is right. **Cultural relativism** asks us first to understand these customs in their own context. Something that seems strange or odd to us can make good sense in another society. The opposite is **ethnocentrism**. This means treating your own culture as the only correct standard.

Two forms are distinguished. **Methodological** cultural relativism is a rule for research: anyone studying a culture should first understand and not judge straight away. **Ethical** cultural relativism goes further and claims that there are no moral standards that apply to all people. The first form is widely accepted in science; the second is highly controversial.

The German-American ethnologist **Franz Boas** is considered its founder. His student **Ruth Benedict** made the idea that every culture forms its own patterns well known with her book “Patterns of Culture” from 1934. **Melville Herskovits** stated cultural relativism especially clearly and studied African and African American cultures. In 1984 Clifford Geertz defended the idea in his lecture “Anti Anti-Relativism”.

In 1956 Horace Miner wrote the satirical essay “Body Ritual among the Nacirema”. In it he describes a supposedly foreign people with strange rituals in front of a shrine in the bathroom. Only when you read carefully do you notice: **Nacirema** is “American” spelt backwards, and what he means is the tooth-brushing and body care of Americans. The text shows how strange even your own habits seem when you look at them from outside.

In 1947 the **American Anthropological Association** warned the UN not to make the values of a single culture the general standard in the planned declaration of human rights. Critics object that radical cultural relativism could excuse oppression or violence as a cultural peculiarity. Most experts today combine both: they want to understand other cultures and still hold on to **human rights**. In multilingual and diverse Switzerland, too, it is important to meet one another with respect and curiosity.

begriffe.erklaerung: The science that studies the cultures and ways of life of people all over the world.
The attitude of taking your own culture as the standard for all others.
Basic rights that every person has, no matter where they live.
A text that uses exaggeration and humour to criticise or expose something.

gewusst: The Nacirema essay is still read in many introductory courses in ethnology today.
As a young researcher, Franz Boas lived with the Inuit on Baffin Island in Canada.

teile.einleitung: The Lotka-Volterra rules describe how the numbers of predators and their prey affect each other. When there are many hares, lynxes find plenty of food and multiply, after which the hares become fewer again. The rules come from a mathematical model developed about 100 years ago.
wichtigste: The rules go back to Alfred Lotka and Vito Volterra.
They describe how the numbers of predators and prey rise and fall together.
Without predators, the prey would grow exponentially in the basic model.
The number of predators follows the number of prey with some delay.
After both species are reduced equally strongly, the prey recovers faster than the predator.
A well-known example is the Canada lynx and the snowshoe hare, with a cycle of about 10 years.
If you plot predators against prey, you get a closed curve around a point of balance.

abschnitte.text: The Lotka-Volterra rules are statements from **ecology**, the study of how living things relate to their environment. They are based on two equations that the American Alfred Lotka in 1925 and the Italian Vito Volterra in 1926 drew up independently of each other. The equations describe a **predator-prey relationship**, for example foxes and mice. The model is greatly simplified, but it shows important basic patterns.

Volterra was prompted by a question from his future son-in-law, the marine biologist Umberto D'Ancona. D'Ancona had studied **fishing data** from the Adriatic after the First World War. During the war there had been hardly any fishing, and afterwards there were noticeably more predatory fish than before. Volterra explained this with his mathematical model.

The **first rule** says that predators and prey rise and fall regularly, with the predators lagging behind the prey in time. The **second rule** says that the average numbers of both species stay the same over a long time. The **third rule** says that after both species are reduced equally strongly, the prey recovers faster than the predator. If you plot the number of predators against the number of prey on a graph, you get a closed loop.

The most famous example comes from Canada. There, over many decades, the Hudson's Bay Company bought furs from hunters, and from these lists the numbers of **Canada lynxes** and **snowshoe hares** could be estimated. Both species rise and fall in a cycle of about 10 years. Today, however, we know that the hares' food and other predators also influence this cycle.

The third rule is important in farming, for example. If a field is sprayed with an insecticide, pests and useful predators such as ladybirds die alike. Afterwards the pests multiply again faster than their enemies and can even become more common than before. That is why today people often use **biological pest control**, in which natural enemies are spared.

begriffe.erklaerung: All the animals of one species that live together in an area.
Growth in which a number gets bigger faster and faster, for example by doubling again and again.
A large reduction in a number.
The science of how living things relate to one another and to their environment.

gewusst: The fur lists of the Hudson's Bay Company go back about 100 years and are valuable research data today.
The Lotka-Volterra equations are also used in economics and chemistry.

teile.einleitung: Food preservation means treating food so that it keeps for longer. People have been drying, salting, smoking and cooling their supplies for thousands of years. The main aim is always to slow down the growth of bacteria, yeasts and moulds.
wichtigste: Food goes bad because microorganisms such as bacteria and moulds grow in it.
Preserving is meant to slow down the growth of these microorganisms.
Salt and sugar draw out of bacteria the water they need to live.
Acid, for example vinegar, slows down bacteria.
Cooling slows down the multiplication of most bacteria.
Nicolas Appert is considered the inventor of preserving food by heating it in airtight containers.
Smoking, drying and salting are among the oldest methods.

abschnitte.text: All around us there are tiny **microorganisms** such as bacteria, yeasts and moulds. They need water, nutrients, warmth and often oxygen to grow. On bread, meat or fruit they find exactly that. In doing so they change the taste and appearance, and some produce toxins. So preserving means taking away at least one of the things they need to live.

In **drying**, fruit, vegetables or meat are dried, and without water germs can hardly grow. Salt works in a similar way: it draws the water out of the bacteria, which is why salted fish keeps for a long time. In jam, a lot of sugar binds the water, so it goes off only slowly despite the fruit. In the Grisons, beef is salted and air-dried, which makes the well-known **Bündnerfleisch**.

Gherkins pickled in vinegar keep for a long time because the **acid** slows down bacteria. In **smoking**, meat or fish is hung in the smoke of smouldering wood, which contains substances against germs and dries the food out. In **fermentation**, useful bacteria help out: they turn white cabbage into sauerkraut and milk into yoghurt. The lactic acid that is produced protects against harmful germs.

Around 1800 the French cook **Nicolas Appert** found out that food keeps for a long time in airtight, heated containers. In 1810 he published his method and received a prize from the French government for it. Soon afterwards tin cans were used too. Later Louis Pasteur explained that heat kills the germs. **Pasteurisation**, which is used for example to make milk keep longer, is named after him.

In the fridge, most bacteria multiply much more slowly, but they do not die. In the freezer, at about minus 18 degrees Celsius, they do not grow at all. In **vacuum packing**, the air is removed, and many germs that need oxygen hardly grow. Some foods also contain permitted **preservatives**, which are listed on the packaging with E numbers.

Do not set the fridge too warm; about 5 degrees Celsius is enough for most foods. Keep raw meat separate from other food. The best-before date does not mean that a food is bad straight afterwards; often you can still check it and eat it. This helps to avoid **food waste**.

begriffe.erklaerung: Tiny living things such as bacteria and fungi that you can only see with a microscope.
Removing water from food so that germs have no more water.
Brief heating that kills many germs, named after Louis Pasteur.
The change of food by useful bacteria or yeasts.
An additive that makes food keep for longer.

gewusst: If stored well, honey can keep for years because it contains so little free water.
Nicolas Appert developed his method because France was looking for food that would keep for soldiers and sailors.
The first tin cans were so thick that you had to open them with a hammer and chisel.

teile.einleitung: An artificial neural network is a computer program built loosely on the model of the brain. It consists of many small computing units, the artificial neurons, which are connected to each other in layers. Such networks are found today in voice assistants, translation programs and chatbots.
wichtigste: An artificial neural network consists of many connected artificial neurons.
Each neuron adds up its inputs multiplied by weights, adds a bias and applies an activation function.
The activation function brings non-linearity into the network; otherwise it could only represent very simple relationships.
At the end of the 1950s Frank Rosenblatt presented an early model, the perceptron.
During learning, the backpropagation algorithm calculates the gradients of the error for all the weights.
In gradient descent, the weights are moved against the gradient at each step.
Networks with many layers are called deep networks, and learning with them is called deep learning.

abschnitte.text: In the human brain there are many billions of **nerve cells**, which exchange signals through connections. An artificial neural network imitates this principle in a much simplified way. Instead of real cells there are only numbers and calculation rules in the computer. The networks are arranged in **layers**: an input layer, one or more hidden layers and an output layer.

An artificial neuron receives several numbers as input. Each input is multiplied by a **weight**, then everything is added up and a **bias** is added. Example: with the weights 2 and -1, the inputs 3 and 4 and a bias of 1, this gives 6 minus 4 plus 1, which is 3. Then comes the activation function, for example **ReLU**: it lets positive numbers through and turns negative numbers into 0, so -3 becomes 0.

At the start the weights are random and the network makes many mistakes. You show it examples with the correct answer and measure how big the error is. The **backpropagation** algorithm works backwards from the output to calculate how each weight affects the error. In **gradient descent**, the weights are then moved a little in the direction in which the error gets smaller. It is like a walker in fog who always goes a little way downhill until reaching the valley.

The weights and bias values together are called **parameters**. A fully connected layer with 10 inputs and 5 neurons has 50 weights and 5 bias values, so 55 parameters. Large language models today have billions of parameters. That is why training needs huge amounts of data and powerful graphics processors in data centres.

In 1958 Frank Rosenblatt presented the **perceptron**, a simple learning machine with one layer. In 1969 Marvin Minsky and Seymour Papert showed that a single-layer perceptron cannot learn the simple function **XOR**. Only with several layers and backpropagation, which became known from 1986, did research really move on. From 2012 deep networks achieved a breakthrough in image recognition. In 2024 John Hopfield and Geoffrey Hinton received the Nobel Prize in Physics for their fundamental work.

Neural networks recognise faces in photos and turn spoken language into text. They translate texts, suggest videos and help doctors analyse X-ray images. The **universal approximation theorem** says that even a network with one hidden layer can approximate any continuous function as closely as you like. In practice, however, deep networks with many layers usually work better.

begriffe.erklaerung: A small computing unit in the network that adds numbers together and passes them on.
A number that decides how much an input counts.
A calculation rule that decides what a neuron outputs, for example ReLU.
A method that traces the error backwards through the network and so gives each weight its share.
Learning with neural networks that have a great many layers.

gewusst: Rosenblatt's first perceptron was a real machine with cables and motors that learned to tell simple pictures apart.
Without an activation function, a network with many layers would be no cleverer than a network with a single layer.
A neural network does not know what it is doing; it only finds patterns in numbers.

teile.einleitung: Louis Pasteur was a French chemist and one of the most important researchers in the history of medicine. He put forward the germ theory, according to which many diseases are caused by tiny living things, the microorganisms. His discoveries still save millions of lives today.
wichtigste: Louis Pasteur lived in France from 1822 to 1895.
He put forward the germ theory: microorganisms cause diseases.
He proved that living things do not simply arise out of nothing.
Pasteurisation, which makes food keep, is named after him.
He developed vaccines, among others against rabies.
In 1885 he saved a small boy with his rabies vaccine.
The Pasteur Institute in Paris bears his name.

abschnitte.text: Louis Pasteur was born on 27 December 1822 in Dole in eastern France. His father was a tanner, a craftsman who made leather. Pasteur studied **chemistry** in Paris and later became a professor. Early on he made an important discovery about crystals of tartaric acid. He died on 28 September 1895 near Paris.

In the past, people did not know where infectious diseases came from. Many believed in bad air or in an imbalance of the body's fluids. Pasteur showed that tiny **microorganisms** such as bacteria cause fermentation, rotting and diseases. This idea is called the **germ theory**. Together with the German doctor Robert Koch, who continued his work, he is considered a founder of modern microbiology.

At that time many people believed in **spontaneous generation**, the idea that tiny living things simply appear by themselves in broth or meat. Pasteur boiled a nutrient broth in a glass flask with a long, curved neck that looked like a swan's neck. Air could get in, but dust and germs got stuck in the bend. The broth stayed clear and fresh for months. In this way he proved that germs come from outside and do not arise by themselves.

Pasteur found out that wine and beer go sour because unwanted microorganisms grow in them. He suggested heating the drinks briefly to kill these germs. This method is named after him: **pasteurisation**. Today it is used above all for milk, so that it keeps longer and does not spread diseases. Fruit juices are also often pasteurised.

Pasteur developed vaccines against animal diseases such as chicken cholera and anthrax. His most famous vaccine was against **rabies**, a deadly disease passed on through animal bites. In 1885 he treated nine-year-old Joseph Meister, who had been bitten by a rabid dog. The boy survived, and Pasteur became world-famous. With donations from all over the world, the **Pasteur Institute** opened in Paris in 1888, and it still researches diseases today.

begriffe.erklaerung: A living thing so small that you can only see it with a microscope, for example a bacterium.
The discovery that many diseases are caused by microorganisms.
Briefly heating food such as milk so that germs are killed.
A treatment that prepares the body for a disease so that it can defend itself better.
The false old idea that living things arise by themselves from dead matter.

gewusst: Joseph Meister, the boy saved by Pasteur, later worked as a caretaker at the Pasteur Institute.
Pasteur had a stroke at the age of 45, but still carried on researching for almost three decades.

teile.einleitung: An index fossil is a fossil that can be used to work out the age of layers of rock. Good index fossils come from living things that existed for only a short time but were widespread. If you find them, you know at once which period of Earth's history a rock comes from.
wichtigste: Index fossils are used to date layers of rock.
A good index fossil lived only for a short time but was widespread.
Trilobites are important index fossils of the Palaeozoic era.
Graptolites are important index fossils of the Ordovician and Silurian.
Tiny foraminifera often serve as index fossils in drill cores.
Around 1800 the Englishman William Smith realised that layers can be matched by their fossils.
Index fossils give a relative age, meaning older or younger.

abschnitte.text: A **fossil** is a remain or trace of a living thing from prehistoric times that has turned to stone. An **index fossil** is a special fossil that is typical of a particular section of Earth's history. It works like a date stamp in the rock. If you find the same index fossil in two places far apart, the layers are about the same age.

abschnitte.titel: What makes a good index fossil?
abschnitte.text: A good index fossil comes from a species that lived only for a short time and changed quickly. At the same time it was widespread, often in the seas of the whole world. It should be common, easily preserved and easy to recognise. Sea creatures are especially suitable, because mud is constantly being laid down on the sea floor and buries them. Land animals such as dinosaurs were preserved much more rarely and are therefore usually poorer index fossils.

**Trilobites** were arthropods with a three-part shell and are important index fossils of the Palaeozoic era. **Graptolites** were small sea creatures that formed colonies; their remains look like pencil marks on slate, and they mark the Ordovician and Silurian. For the Mesozoic era, meaning the Jurassic and Cretaceous, the **ammonites** with their spiral shells are especially important. Tiny single-celled organisms with lime shells, the foraminifera, are found in their thousands in drill cores.

Around 1800 the English surveyor **William Smith** worked on building canals. He noticed that each layer of rock contains its own typical fossils. This allowed him to match layers even in places far apart. In 1815 he published one of the first geological maps of a whole country. That is why he is also called the father of English geology.

With index fossils you can say which layer is older or younger; this is called **relative dating**. But it does not give an exact number of years. For that, absolute dating with radioactive substances in the rock is used today. The two methods together make up the geological time scale. Oil and mining companies also use index fossils to identify layers of rock in boreholes.

In the Swiss Jura you find many ammonites from the time when a warm sea lay here. The Jurassic period is even named after the Jura mountains. In the Alps there are the coin-shaped **nummulites**, single-celled organisms that are considered index fossils for the early Paleogene. Monte San Giorgio in Ticino is world-famous for its fossils from the Triassic and is a UNESCO World Natural Heritage site.

begriffe.erklaerung: A remain or imprint of a living thing from prehistoric times that has turned to stone.
A layer of rock that was laid down over a long time.
Working out whether something is older or younger, without an exact date.
An extinct arthropod of the Palaeozoic era with a three-part shell.
An extinct sea creature with a spiral shell, related to squid and octopuses.

gewusst: Some ammonite species lived for only a few hundred thousand years, which makes them very precise time markers.
Trilobites were among the first animals with real eyes, which were made of lime crystals.
The name graptolite means writing stone, because the fossils look like written characters on the rock.

teile.einleitung: In autumn, green woods turn into a sea of yellow, orange and red. This change of leaf colour is no accident but a clever plan by the trees to prepare for winter. In the process they take valuable substances back out of the leaves before these fall.
wichtigste: The signal for the leaves to change colour is the shortening days.
Trees break down the green pigment chlorophyll and take back valuable nutrients.
Then yellow and orange pigments become visible, which were already in the leaf before.
Some trees make new red pigments in autumn.
A separation layer forms at the leaf stalk, and then the leaf falls.
With sunny days and cool nights, the leaves become especially colourful.
In the mountains the trees change colour earlier, because it gets cold there earlier.

abschnitte.text: In summer, leaves are green because they contain a lot of **chlorophyll**. With this pigment they use sunlight to make sugar, which is called photosynthesis. In winter this would be difficult, because it is cold and dark and the ground is often frozen. Broad leaves would also give off a lot of water, which the tree cannot replace from the frozen ground. That is why deciduous trees shed their leaves.

When the days get shorter, the tree starts to break down the chlorophyll and to take its building blocks, such as nitrogen, back into the branches and roots. Now the yellow and orange **carotenoids** become visible, which were in the leaf all year but were covered by the green. The same orange pigment is also found in carrots. Some trees, such as maples, also make new red **anthocyanins**. If a leaf lies on the ground for a long time, it usually turns brown, because tannins are left over.

At the base of the leaf stalk, the tree forms a **separation layer** of cork cells. It gradually cuts the leaf off from its water supply and seals the wound. In the end a gust of wind is enough, and the leaf falls. Young **beeches** often keep their dry brown leaves until spring, and you can hear them rustling in winter.

The leaves become especially colourful with sunny days and cool nights. Then a lot of sugar forms in the leaf, from which red pigments are made. In the mountains the trees change colour earlier than in the valley, because it gets cold there earlier. The forests in the north-east of the USA and in Canada are famous for their autumn colours, where people talk of an **Indian summer**.

Spruces and firs keep their needles in winter. The needles are narrow and protected by a layer of wax, so they lose little water. An exception is the **larch**: it turns golden yellow in autumn and sheds its needles. In the Engadine and in Valais, whole larch forests glow like gold in October.

In Switzerland the leaves in the Central Plateau usually start changing colour in October. Beeches glow copper-red, birches and maples yellow, and cherry trees often red. Autumn walks in the Jura, in Ticino or along the larch paths in the Upper Engadine are popular. The fallen leaves are important for the soil, because **soil organisms** turn them into fertile humus.

begriffe.erklaerung: The green leaf pigment with which plants use sunlight.
Yellow and orange pigments that are also found in carrots.
Red to purple pigments that some trees make new in autumn.
A layer at the leaf stalk where the leaf comes away from the twig.
The process in which plants use light to make sugar from water and carbon dioxide.

gewusst: The yellow pigments are already in the leaf in summer; you just cannot see them because of all the green.
The larch is the only native conifer in Switzerland that loses its needles in autumn.
A large deciduous tree can shed tens of thousands of leaves in autumn.

teile.einleitung: The Cretaceous-Paleogene boundary marks the end of the Cretaceous period about 66 million years ago. At that time a huge asteroid struck the Earth, and about three quarters of all animal and plant species died out. The dinosaurs disappeared too, except for the birds.
wichtigste: The boundary lies about 66 million years in the past.
An asteroid about 10 kilometres across struck the Yucatán Peninsula in Mexico.
A lot of iridium is found in the thin layer of clay at the boundary.
Dust darkened the Sun, so many plants died.
The impact set off enormous tsunamis.
The volcanic eruptions of the Deccan Traps in India are thought to be a possible additional cause.
Birds were the only group of dinosaurs to survive.
Afterwards mammals spread widely.

abschnitte.text: Geologists divide the history of the Earth into periods. The **Cretaceous** ended about 66 million years ago, and then the **Paleogene** began. The boundary between the two can be seen in many rocks as a thin, dark layer of clay. It used to be called the K-T boundary. It marks one of the five biggest mass extinctions in the history of the Earth.

An asteroid with a diameter of about 10 kilometres hurtled towards the Earth. It struck the Yucatán Peninsula in Mexico and left the **Chicxulub crater**, about 180 kilometres across. Today the crater lies hidden under rock and sea. The explosion was millions of times stronger than any atomic bomb. It set off earthquakes, fires and giant tsunamis.

In 1980 the physicist Luis Alvarez and his son, the geologist Walter Alvarez, discovered a lot of **iridium** in the boundary layer. This metal is very rare in the Earth's crust but more common in asteroids. So they suspected an impact from space. Only about ten years later was the matching crater found in Mexico.

The impact hurled huge amounts of dust, soot and sulphur into the air. These clouds darkened the Sun for months or years. Plants could hardly carry out **photosynthesis** any more and died. As a result, the plant-eaters and then the meat-eaters could no longer find food. At the same time, in India, the volcanoes of the **Deccan Traps** poured out huge amounts of lava, which put extra strain on the climate.

All dinosaurs except the birds died out, as did the pterosaurs and the large marine reptiles. The **ammonites**, sea creatures with spiral shells, disappeared too. Small animals that could hide or eat seeds and carrion had better chances. Birds are direct descendants of dinosaurs and are therefore the only ones still alive today.

After the extinction, many habitats were suddenly free. The **mammals**, which until then had mostly been small, spread quickly and developed many new forms. From them later came whales, horses, apes and finally humans. Without the impact, the animal world would probably look very different today.

begriffe.erklaerung: A time when a very large number of species on Earth die out within a short period.
A rare, heavy metal that is more common in asteroids than on Earth.
A lump of rock that orbits the Sun.
The period of Earth's history that began directly after the Cretaceous.
A huge area of solidified lava in the west of India.

gewusst: A chicken is more closely related to Tyrannosaurus than a crocodile is.
The boundary layer is often only a few centimetres thick, yet it tells of one of the biggest disasters in the history of the Earth.
The name Cretaceous comes from the Latin word for chalk: white chalk cliffs formed in this period from tiny lime shells.

teile.einleitung: Solubility describes how well a substance dissolves in a liquid. When you stir sugar into warm water, it dissolves and seems to disappear, but afterwards the water tastes sweet. Some substances dissolve very well, others not at all, like oil in water.
wichtigste: Solubility tells you how much of a substance dissolves in a liquid.
Sugar and salt dissolve well in water.
Oil and sand do not dissolve in water.
A solution that cannot take in any more is called saturated.
Solids usually dissolve better in warm water.
Gases, on the other hand, dissolve better in cold water.
Water is the most important solvent on Earth.

abschnitte.text: When a substance spreads out in a liquid until you can no longer see it, this is called **dissolving**. The liquid is called the **solvent**, and the mixture is called a solution. **Solubility** tells you the most of a substance that can dissolve in a certain amount of solvent. The substance has not disappeared; it has only broken up into tiny particles. If you let the water evaporate, it appears again.

Sugar is made of tiny particles called molecules. The water particles surround these molecules and pull them one by one out of the sugar crystal. In warm water the particles move faster, so sugar dissolves faster there and in larger amounts. Stirring also helps, because fresh water keeps reaching the sugar. At 20 degrees, about 200 grams of sugar dissolve in 100 grams of water, but only about 36 grams of table salt.

If you keep adding more and more salt to a glass of water, at some point nothing more dissolves. The rest of the salt stays lying at the bottom. Then the solution is **saturated**. If a saturated solution cools down or water evaporates, crystals form again. In this way you can grow sugar or salt crystals at home.

With gases it is the other way round from sugar: they dissolve better in **cold water** than in warm water. That is why warm mineral water fizzes more and loses its fizz faster. Fish in warm lakes sometimes have too little oxygen in summer, because warm water contains less of it. Oil does not dissolve in water at all and floats on top. Chemists say “like dissolves like”, so fat dissolves in oil or petrol, but not in water.

Our body uses water as a solvent to carry nutrients in the blood. When washing up, washing-up liquid helps to spread fat out in the water. In Switzerland, the **Swiss Saltworks** obtain salt by pumping water into deep layers of salt, where it dissolves the salt. The salty brine is pumped back up, and the water is evaporated until salt is left. In caves, water containing carbonic acid dissolves limestone and later lets it crystallise again as **stalactites and stalagmites**.

begriffe.erklaerung: A liquid in which another substance dissolves, for example water.
A mixture in which a substance is very finely spread out in a liquid.
So full of dissolved substance that nothing more can dissolve.
Water in which a great deal of salt is dissolved.

gewusst: So much salt is dissolved in seawater that a litre contains about 35 grams of salt.
Water dissolves so many different substances that it is often called the “universal solvent”.

teile.einleitung: Kurt Wüthrich is a Swiss chemist who received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2002. He developed a method that makes the shape of proteins visible. For this he used nuclear magnetic resonance, NMR for short.
wichtigste: Kurt Wüthrich was born in 1938 in Aarberg in the canton of Bern.
He did most of his research at ETH Zurich.
His method determines the three-dimensional structure of proteins with NMR.
In 1984 his group determined the complete structure of a protein with NMR for the first time.
In 2002 he received half of the Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
The other half went to John Fenn and Koichi Tanaka for the mass spectrometry of large biomolecules.
He also worked at the Scripps Research Institute in California.

abschnitte.text: Kurt Wüthrich was born on 4 October 1938 in the small Bernese town of **Aarberg**. He studied chemistry, physics and mathematics at the University of Bern. He gained his doctorate at the University of Basel. After that he did research in the USA for a few years before returning to Switzerland.

From 1969 Wüthrich worked at **ETH Zurich**, where he later became professor of biophysics. There he built up a well-known research group over decades. From 2001 he also did research at the **Scripps Research Institute** in La Jolla, California. So he travelled back and forth between Zurich and the USA.

NMR stands for **nuclear magnetic resonance**, a measuring method using very strong magnets and radio waves. Certain atomic nuclei, above all hydrogen nuclei, behave like tiny compass needles in a magnetic field. With radio waves you can excite them and measure their signals. From these signals you can read which atoms lie close to one another. The same technology is also used in the MRI scanner in hospital.

**Proteins** are long chains that fold into a very particular shape, and this shape decides their job in the body. In the past, the shape could only be determined if the protein was made into a crystal. Wüthrich showed that NMR can also determine the structure in a liquid, which is how proteins occur in the body. In 1984 his group achieved the first complete protein structure with this method.

For his method, Wüthrich received half of the **Nobel Prize** in Chemistry in 2002. The other half was shared by John Fenn and Koichi Tanaka, who had studied large biomolecules with mass spectrometry. Wüthrich also worked out the structure of the **prion protein**, which plays a role in diseases such as BSE, mad cow disease. Today his method is used in laboratories all over the world in research on medicines.

begriffe.erklaerung: Nuclear magnetic resonance, a measuring method using magnets and radio waves that examines atoms inside substances.
A building block of the body that carries out many tasks.
A wrongly folded protein that can cause diseases such as BSE.
One of the most famous science prizes in the world, awarded every year in Stockholm.

gewusst: When Kurt Wüthrich received the Nobel Prize, he was 64 years old.
The magnets in NMR machines are many thousands of times stronger than the Earth's magnetic field.

teile.einleitung: A lab coat is a coat, usually white, that you wear when working in a laboratory. It protects skin and clothes from chemicals, dirt and germs. For many people it has become the sign of a researcher.
wichtigste: A lab coat protects skin and clothes.
Lab coats are usually white.
Many are made of cotton, because it does not melt onto the skin in a fire.
The sleeves reach down to the wrist.
In the laboratory you wear the coat fastened.
Press studs let you take the coat off quickly in an emergency.
You take it off before you leave the laboratory.

abschnitte.text: The **lab coat** is a long coat that usually reaches below the knees. It is part of the **protective equipment** in the laboratory, together with safety goggles and gloves. It is worn in chemistry labs, in biology, in hospitals and in food inspection. In school labs, too, young people often put on a coat for experiments.

In experiments, acids, alkalis or dyes can splash. The coat catches such splashes before they reach skin or clothing. In biological labs it keeps **germs** away from your own clothes. That is why you take it off before leaving the laboratory, so that nothing is carried outside. Dirty coats are washed separately or thrown away.

Many lab coats are made of **cotton** or a mixture with synthetic fibres. Cotton does burn, but it does not melt and so does not stick to the skin in a fire. For work with fire or flammable substances there are also flame-resistant coats. The long sleeves reach down to the wrist and often have tight cuffs. **Press studs** can be pulled open with one tug if the coat has to come off quickly in an emergency.

You always wear the coat fastened, otherwise it does not protect the clothes underneath. Long hair is tied back, and you wear sturdy, closed shoes. There is no eating or drinking in the laboratory. **Safety goggles** are compulsory for many experiments, because the eyes are especially sensitive.

On white fabric you can see stains and dirt at once. White has also stood for cleanliness and **hygiene** for a long time. Since the end of the 19th century, doctors have also often worn a white coat. In some areas there are also coloured coats, such as blue or green, for example in the operating theatre.

In films, comics and adverts you can often recognise researchers at once by their white coat. It has become a **symbol** of science and expert knowledge. But in many researchers' daily work it is not always needed, for example at the computer or at physics measuring instruments. It really matters where people work with chemicals, samples or living cells.

begriffe.erklaerung: A room in which experts carry out experiments and examine samples.
Clothing and equipment that protect the body from dangers at work.
A fastener made of two parts that opens at once when pulled.
Measures for cleanliness so that diseases do not spread.

gewusst: Because press studs can be ripped open with one tug, a lab coat can be taken off in a second.
Doctors used to wear black clothing; the white coat only caught on with modern hygiene.
In some schools, young people get their first lab coat in chemistry lessons.

teile.einleitung: The litre is a unit of volume, which means how much fits into a container. Milk, water, petrol and squash are measured in litres. One litre is exactly the same as a cube with edges 10 centimetres long.
wichtigste: The litre is abbreviated l.
One litre has 10 decilitres, 100 centilitres or 1000 millilitres.
One litre is exactly as much as one cubic decimetre.
A large PET bottle of mineral water holds 1.5 litres.
A full bath holds about 150 litres of water.
An ordinary drinking glass holds about 2 decilitres.
A cow in Switzerland gives about 25 litres of milk a day.

abschnitte.text: A litre is as much as fits into a cube with edges 10 centimetres long. This cube is also called a **cubic decimetre**, so 1 litre equals 1 dm³. A litre of water weighs almost exactly one kilogram. That is no accident: the kilogram used to be defined by the weight of a litre of water. The litre is not one of the base units, but it is approved worldwide alongside the **cubic metre**.

A litre is divided into smaller units. A **decilitre** is a tenth of a litre; in Switzerland the decilitre is very common in recipes and restaurants. A centilitre is a hundredth of a litre, and a millilitre a thousandth. A millilitre is as much as a cube with edges one centimetre long. Large amounts are measured in hectolitres: 1 hectolitre is 100 litres.

In shops you often find milk in one-litre cartons and mineral water in bottles of 1.5 litres or 5 decilitres. A drinking glass holds about 2 decilitres, and a cleaning bucket about 10 litres. A full bath holds about 150 litres. When doing sums, you can add litres together: 2 litres of squash and 3 litres of water make 5 litres. The fuel consumption of a car is also given in litres per 100 kilometres.

A dairy cow in Switzerland gives about 25 litres of milk a day. A person in Switzerland uses about 140 litres of water a day at home, mainly for the toilet, the shower and the washing machine. A swimming pool 25 metres long contains several hundred thousand litres. For very large amounts of water, for example in reservoirs, people therefore calculate in **cubic metres**. One cubic metre is 1000 litres.

The litre was introduced in France in 1795, when the metric system was created there. The name comes from an older French measure of volume called the “litron”. With the metric system, the litre spread throughout Europe. In Switzerland, old measures such as the Mass and the Saum were replaced by metric units in the 19th century. Today the litre is known almost everywhere in the world; only in the USA do people often still use **gallons** in everyday life.

begriffe.erklaerung: How much space something takes up or how much fits into a container.
A tenth of a litre, abbreviated dl.
A thousandth of a litre, abbreviated ml.
A cube with edges 1 metre long; it holds 1000 litres.

gewusst: Because a small l is easily confused with the number 1, the litre may also be abbreviated with a capital L.
A litre of water weighs about 1 kilogram, but a litre of olive oil weighs less, because oil is lighter than water.
Household water use in Switzerland would fill roughly one full bath per person every day.

teile.einleitung: An alloy is a mixture of a metal with at least one other substance, usually of two or more metals. Mixing them produces a material with new properties, which is, for example, harder or rusts less. Bronze, brass and steel are well-known alloys.
wichtigste: An alloy is a mixture of two or more metals.
Sometimes a non-metal such as carbon is also mixed in.
Alloys have different properties from the pure metals.
Bronze is made of copper and tin.
Brass is made of copper and zinc.
Steel is an alloy of iron with a little carbon.
Swiss coins are also made of alloys.

abschnitte.text: An **alloy** is made when you melt a metal and mix other substances into it. Usually these are other metals, sometimes non-metals such as carbon. When it cools, the mixture becomes solid again. The result looks like a metal and has typical metal properties. But it behaves differently from each of its single parts.

Pure metals are often too soft or rust easily. Pure gold, for example, can almost be bent with a fingernail. When you mix metals, they usually become **harder** and stronger. Some alloys hardly rust or melt at a low temperature, like the solder used for soldering electronics. In this way the right material can be made for every purpose.

**Bronze** is an alloy of copper and a little tin and one of the oldest in the world. It is much harder than pure copper. Because bronze was so important for tools, weapons and jewellery, a whole era is named after it, the **Bronze Age**. In central Europe, including Switzerland, it lasted from about 2200 to 800 BC. Bells and statues are still cast in bronze today.

**Steel** consists of iron and a little carbon and is the most important material for bridges, cars and machines. If you add chromium and nickel, you get rust-free **stainless steel**, from which many saucepans and much cutlery are made. Brass, made of copper and zinc, shines golden yellow and is used for door handles and brass instruments such as trumpets. Light aluminium alloys are needed for aircraft and bike frames. Gold jewellery is almost always an alloy too: 18-carat gold, for example, contains 75 per cent gold.

The Swiss franc coins and the 10 and 20 centime coins are made of an alloy of copper and nickel. The gold-coloured 5 centime coin is made of aluminium bronze. In the Swiss **watch industry**, special alloys are used for cases, springs and gear wheels. Some watch companies have even developed their own gold alloys. So alloys also play a big role in a typically Swiss craft.

begriffe.erklaerung: A mixture of a metal and at least one other substance, usually another metal.
A hard alloy of copper and tin.
An alloy of iron and a little carbon.
Steel that hardly rusts thanks to additions such as chromium.

gewusst: Pure gold is so soft that jewellery made from it would quickly get scratched and bent.
Some alloys, called shape-memory alloys, return to their original shape when warmed after being bent.

teile.einleitung: A laboratory is a room in which researchers do experiments, examine samples and discover new things. It has special equipment such as microscopes, test tubes and scales. The word comes from the Latin “laborare”, which means “to work”.
wichtigste: A laboratory is a workroom for experiments and tests.
There are laboratories for chemistry, biology, medicine, physics and much more.
Typical equipment includes test tubes, pipettes, Bunsen burners and microscopes.
Strict safety rules apply in the laboratory.
Lab coats, safety goggles and gloves protect the people working there.
Many new medicines are developed in laboratories.
One of the largest research laboratories in the world, CERN, is near Geneva.

abschnitte.text: A **laboratory**, or lab, is a room specially equipped for experiments and measurements. Work there is precise, clean and follows fixed rules. Researchers ask a question, plan an **experiment** and write down all the results. Then others check whether they get the same result. This is how reliable knowledge is built up.

In a chemistry lab you find **test tubes**, beakers and conical flasks made of heat-resistant glass. With pipettes you can measure tiny amounts of liquid accurately. The **Bunsen burner**, named after the chemist Robert Bunsen, produces a hot gas flame. Biology and medical labs have microscopes, centrifuges and fridges for samples. Today many labs also have computers and robots that check thousands of samples automatically.

In the laboratory people often work with fire, acids or germs that cause disease. That is why everyone wears a **lab coat**, safety goggles and often gloves. Dangerous fumes are sucked away in a fume cupboard so that nobody breathes them in. Eating and drinking are forbidden in the laboratory. Hazard symbols on bottles show whether a substance is, for example, poisonous or flammable.

There are many kinds of laboratory. In a medical lab, for example, blood samples are examined so that doctors can identify an illness. In a food lab, tests check whether food is clean and safe. At school there is often a science room where pupils do their own experiments. Computer chips even need **clean rooms**, where there is hardly a speck of dust in the air.

Near Geneva lies **CERN**, the European Organization for Nuclear Research, which was founded in 1954. There, thousands of researchers from all over the world study the smallest particles. In Aargau there is the Paul Scherrer Institute, the largest research institute for natural sciences and engineering in Switzerland. In Basel, pharmaceutical companies run large laboratories where medicines are developed. ETH Zurich and EPFL in Lausanne also have many research labs.

begriffe.erklaerung: A planned test used to check a question.
A narrow glass tube in which small amounts of substances are mixed or heated.
A gas burner that produces a hot, adjustable flame in the laboratory.
A room with especially clean air, with almost no dust.

gewusst: The World Wide Web was invented at CERN in 1989 so that researchers could share their results more easily.
The discovery of penicillin began in 1928 when Alexander Fleming noticed a mouldy dish of bacteria in his laboratory.

teile.einleitung: The lotus effect describes how some plant leaves keep themselves clean. Water forms round beads, rolls off and takes the dirt with it. The effect is named after the lotus plant, whose leaves always look clean even in a muddy pond.
wichtigste: On a lotus leaf, water beads up and takes dirt with it.
This is called self-cleaning.
The surface of the leaf has tiny bumps and is coated with wax.
A drop rests on the tips of the bumps above trapped cushions of air.
Nasturtiums also show a strong lotus effect.
If the fine structures are rubbed away, the effect is lost.
The lotus effect is used in bionics for paints and coatings.

abschnitte.text: The **lotus plant** grows in water, mainly in Asia, and has large round leaves above the water's surface. When rain falls on them, round drops form and roll off straight away. As they do so, they take dust and dirt with them, and the leaf cleans itself. This **self-cleaning** is called the lotus effect.

Under an electron microscope you can see that the lotus leaf is covered with **tiny bumps**. These bumps are also coated with even finer **wax crystals**; scientists speak of **micro- and nanostructures**. A drop of water touches only the tips and rests on a cushion of trapped air. This state is called the Cassie-Baxter state. Dirt particles hardly stick either, and they cling to the drop instead of to the leaf.

How strongly a surface repels water is shown by the **contact angle** between the drop and the surface. If it is below 90 degrees, the surface counts as **hydrophilic**, and water wets it well. On the lotus leaf the angle is greater than 150 degrees, and the drop is almost a sphere. Such surfaces are called **superhydrophobic**. If the water fills the hollows instead, this is called the Wenzel state, and the drop sticks more strongly.

In Swiss gardens, the **nasturtium** shows a very strong lotus effect, and cabbage leaves also let water bead off well. The **pond skater** can walk on water thanks to water-repellent hairs on its legs. A floating fern holds a layer of air on its leaves under water with what is called the **Salvinia effect**. In the rose petal effect, drops stay stuck to the petal despite a large contact angle.

The German botanist **Wilhelm Barthlott** studied the effect from the 1970s at the University of Bonn and gave it its name. Following this model, there are now **facade paints** from which rain washes off the dirt. Roof tiles, textiles and glass are also coated in this way. Because the fine structures are delicate, the effect is lost if the surface is rubbed hard.

You can watch the lotus effect at home. Sprinkle a little dust or cocoa powder on a nasturtium leaf and then drip some water onto it. The drops roll off and collect the powder. If you rub the leaf with your finger, the water beads off less well at that spot.

begriffe.erklaerung: A surface stays clean because water takes the dirt away with it.
Water-repellent: water forms round drops.
Water-loving: water spreads out flat.
The angle that a drop makes with the surface it is lying on.

gewusst: In Asia, because of its clean leaves, the lotus flower is a symbol of purity in several religions.
In Japan there are yoghurt lids with a water-repellent coating modelled on the lotus leaf, to which hardly any yoghurt sticks.

teile.einleitung: Toads are amphibians with a sturdy body, short legs and warty skin. Many people find them creepy, but they are harmless and very useful snail hunters. In Switzerland the common toad is the best-known species.
wichtigste: Like frogs and newts, toads are amphibians.
Their skin is usually drier and bumpier than that of frogs.
The bumps on the skin are glands that can release a defensive poison.
If you touch a toad you do not get warts, because warts are caused by viruses.
Common toads like to eat snails, insects, worms and spiders.
In spring many toads migrate to the waters where they spawn.
Small fences along roads protect the migrating toads from traffic.

abschnitte.text: Toads have a stocky body, a broad snout and rather short hind legs. That is why they hop less than frogs and prefer to walk slowly. Their skin is dry and covered with many bumps, which are **skin glands**. Behind the eyes there are two large swellings, the **parotoid glands**. The eyes of the common toad glow copper-red to golden.

When a toad is attacked, its glands give off a milky, bitter slime. It contains poisons called **bufotoxins**. For people the poison is harmless after normal touching, but you should wash your hands afterwards. Dogs that take a toad in their mouth can become ill. The idea that toads give you warts is an old mistake, because warts are caused by **viruses**.

For most of the year toads live on land, for example in woods, gardens, meadows and cellars. During the day they hide under stones, leaves or wood and go hunting at dusk. They eat snails, beetles, woodlice, worms and spiders. This makes them welcome helpers in the vegetable garden. They spend the winter in **hibernation** in frost-free hiding places.

In spring, when the nights become milder and damp, common toads migrate to the pond where they themselves hatched. This **toad migration** often crosses roads, where many animals are run over. Volunteers therefore put up low fences that the toads walk along until they fall into buckets. In the morning, helpers carry the buckets safely across the road. Some roads also have permanent **toad tunnels**.

In the pond, common toads lay long strings of spawn among the water plants. Small black **tadpoles** hatch from them and breathe in the water with gills. After a few weeks they grow legs, the tail disappears, and they turn into tiny toads. In summer the young toads leave the pond in their thousands.

The common toad, the natterjack toad and the green toad live in Switzerland. The **natterjack toad** has a yellow stripe on its back and needs small, warm pools, for example in gravel pits. Because many wetlands have disappeared, the natterjack toad and the green toad are considered endangered. All amphibians are protected in Switzerland, and you are not allowed to catch or kill them.

begriffe.erklaerung: Animals that live first in water and later mostly on land, for example frogs, toads and newts.
The larva of frogs and toads, which lives in water and has a tail.
Eggs of amphibians or fish that are laid in water.
Poisons from the skin glands of toads.

gewusst: Toads often return to exactly the same water in which they grew up as tadpoles.
The cane toad was released in Australia in 1935 and has become a huge pest there.
Toads do not drink with their mouths but take in water through their skin.

teile.einleitung: Lidar is a measuring method that scans the surroundings with laser light and creates exact three-dimensional pictures from this. With lidar you can even measure the ground through forests. This is how researchers have discovered hidden ruins of ancient cultures that were concealed under the jungle.
wichtigste: Lidar stands for “Light Detection and Ranging”.
A lidar device sends out laser pulses and measures how long the light takes to reach the target and come back.
All the measuring points together are called a point cloud.
For large areas, lidar data are usually collected from aircraft or helicopters.
Some pulses reach the ground through gaps in the leaves, so measurements can be made even under forest.
From the ground points, a digital terrain model without vegetation and buildings is calculated.
In 2018, lidar revealed tens of thousands of unknown Maya structures in northern Guatemala.

abschnitte.text: Lidar is the abbreviation for **Light Detection and Ranging**, roughly “detecting and measuring distance with light”. It works much like radar, only with laser light instead of radio waves. A device sends out very short **laser pulses**, often hundreds of thousands a second. From these, an exact 3D image of land, buildings or trees is created.

Light travels at about 300,000 kilometres a second. The device measures the time it takes for a laser pulse to be reflected by an object and come back. From this **travel time** it calculates the distance. Together with the exact position, which is found by satellite navigation, each hit gives a point in space. All the points together make a **point cloud**.

When measuring from aircraft or helicopters, many pulses hit the tops of trees. But some get through gaps in the leaves to the **ground**. A computer filters out the ground points and calculates a **digital terrain model**, which shows the Earth's surface without trees and houses. With **hillshading**, meaning artificial light and shadow, even fine shapes in the land become visible.

In 2018 a large lidar campaign in northern **Guatemala** discovered tens of thousands of previously unknown Maya structures, including houses, roads and fortifications. In **Cambodia**, extensive medieval urban landscapes around the temple complex of Angkor were mapped with lidar. In Swiss forests, lidar data often reveal burial mounds, earthworks and old sunken lanes. In this way archaeological sites are found without digging.

The Federal Office of Topography, **swisstopo**, has measured the whole of Switzerland with lidar from the air. This produces very accurate elevation models of the country, which anyone can look at online. They help in planning roads, in protecting against natural hazards such as debris flows and in monitoring glaciers. Foresters also use the data to work out the height and density of forests.

Many self-driving cars and robots use lidar to detect obstacles around them. Some smartphones and tablets have small lidar sensors that can be used to measure rooms. Lidar is also used in research on clouds and air pollution. The technology is getting smaller and cheaper all the time.

begriffe.erklaerung: Concentrated, very precise light of a single colour.
A huge collection of measuring points that together make a 3D image.
A computer model of the Earth's surface without trees and buildings.
A way of showing land with artificial light and shadow so that its shapes look three-dimensional.

gewusst: A lidar aircraft can record hundreds of thousands of measuring points a second.
With lidar, traces of settlements have been discovered in Swiss forests that had been hidden under leaves and moss for centuries.
On the Apollo missions a laser was already used to measure the height above the Moon's surface.

teile.einleitung: The last ice age was a long, cold period of Earth's history that began about 115,000 years ago and ended about 11,700 years ago. At that time, huge glaciers lay over northern Europe, North America and the Alps. Much of the Swiss Central Plateau was also buried under thick ice.
wichtigste: The last ice age ended about 11,700 years ago.
In the Alpine region it is called the Würm glaciation, after a river in Bavaria.
A large part of the Swiss Central Plateau was covered by glacier ice.
The Rhône Glacier carried rock from Valais as far as the area around Solothurn.
Large boulders carried along by the ice are called erratic boulders.
The sea level was about 120 metres lower than today.
Woolly mammoths also lived in Switzerland at that time.

abschnitte.text: Over the last 2.6 million years or so, **cold periods** and **warm periods** have alternated on Earth several times. During the cold periods, huge ice sheets and glaciers grew. The last cold period lasted from about 115,000 to 11,700 years ago. In the Alpine region it is called the **Würm glaciation** after the River Würm in Bavaria, and in northern Germany the Weichselian glaciation. Today we live in a warm period, the Holocene.

At the height of the glaciation, about 20,000 years ago, the Alpine glaciers flowed far out into the Central Plateau. The **Rhône Glacier** reached from Valais over Lake Geneva to the area of Solothurn and Wangen an der Aare. The Reuss Glacier and the Linth Glacier also pushed far to the north. Only the highest peaks stuck out of the ice. When the glaciers retreated, they left behind lakes such as Lake Zurich, Lake Lucerne and Lake Biel.

The glaciers carried boulders over long distances; these are called **erratic boulders**. In the Central Plateau there are many erratics made of granite from Valais, which clearly do not come from the area. At the edges of the glaciers, hills of rubble formed, the **moraines**. Many valleys were also scoured out by the ice and therefore have a typical U shape.

In the cold steppe in front of the glaciers lived **woolly mammoths**, woolly rhinoceroses, reindeer, wild horses and cave bears. In Niederweningen in the canton of Zurich, many mammoth bones were found, which can be seen in a small museum. The animals had thick fur and fat reserves against the cold. Towards the end of the ice age many of these large animals died out.

Because so much water was locked up as ice on land, the sea level was about **120 metres** lower than today. Many areas that are sea today were dry land. Between Asia and North America, the land bridge **Beringia** at the Bering Strait lay exposed. People and animals reached America across it, and Great Britain was also joined to the European mainland.

During the last ice age, first the Neanderthals and later also modern humans lived in Europe. They hunted reindeer and wild horses and lived in caves or in tents made of hides. Famous cave paintings come from this time, such as those in the cave of Lascaux in France. In Switzerland, tools and skilful carvings by ice-age hunters were found in the **Kesslerloch** cave near Thayngen in the canton of Schaffhausen.

begriffe.erklaerung: A long time with a cold climate and large glaciers, also called an ice age.
A warmer period between two cold periods.
A large boulder that a glacier has carried far from where it came from.
A ridge or hill of rubble left behind by a glacier.
A land bridge between Asia and North America that lay dry during the ice age.

gewusst: At the height of the ice age, a layer of ice several hundred metres thick lay over the area of today's city of Bern.
Because Great Britain was joined to the mainland, you could then walk from France to England without getting your feet wet.
Many erratic boulders in the Central Plateau used to be broken up for building material; today some are protected.

teile.einleitung: Leonardo da Vinci was an Italian painter, inventor and researcher of the Renaissance. He painted the famous Mona Lisa and filled thousands of pages with drawings of machines, plants and the human body. That is why many people call him a universal genius.
wichtigste: Leonardo da Vinci lived from 1452 to 1519.
He was born near the small town of Vinci in Italy.
He painted the Mona Lisa and the mural The Last Supper.
He was not only a painter but also an inventor and researcher.
He dreamed of flying and drew flying machines.
To draw people better, he studied muscles and bones.
His drawing Vitruvian Man is world-famous.
He often wrote his notes in mirror writing.

abschnitte.text: Leonardo was born on 15 April 1452 near **Vinci** in Tuscany, hence his name: Leonardo from Vinci. As a young man he went to **Florence** to train with the artist Andrea del Verrocchio. There he learned painting, sculpture and a lot about technology. He lived in the **Renaissance**, a time when art and science flourished in Europe.

The **Mona Lisa** shows a woman with a mysterious smile and hangs today in the Louvre in Paris. It is probably the best-known painting in the world. In Milan, Leonardo painted the huge mural **The Last Supper** in a monastery. Leonardo worked very slowly and thoroughly, so he finished only a few paintings completely.

Leonardo wanted to know exactly how the human body is built. He studied muscles, bones and organs and drew them very accurately. His **anatomy** drawings were far ahead of their time. Also famous is the **Vitruvian Man**, a man with outstretched arms and legs in a circle and a square, which shows the proportions of the body.

Leonardo watched birds and bats to understand how they fly. He drew flying machines with flapping wings, a parachute and a kind of **aerial screw** that is reminiscent of a helicopter. Most of these machines were not built in his time. But his ideas show how far ahead he was thinking.

Leonardo always carried notebooks with him and wrote from right to left in **mirror writing**. In them you find plans for bridges, canals, weapons, diving suits and machines. He also studied water, light, plants and rocks. Today about 7000 pages of his notes still survive.

For a long time Leonardo worked in Milan for Duke **Ludovico Sforza**. Later he lived again in Florence and in Rome. In the end the French king Francis I brought him to France. Leonardo died on 2 May 1519 in Amboise on the Loire.

begriffe.erklaerung: The period from the 14th to the 16th century, when art and science flourished anew in Europe; the word means rebirth.
A person who achieves great things in very many fields.
The science of how the body is built.
Writing that can only be read normally in a mirror.

gewusst: The Mona Lisa is only about 77 centimetres high and 53 centimetres wide, so smaller than many people think.
In 1911 the Mona Lisa was stolen from the Louvre and was only found again in Florence two years later.
Leonardo was left-handed, which made his mirror writing easier.

teile.einleitung: Kitchen scales are a measuring device used to weigh ingredients for cooking and baking. They usually show the weight in grams. If you weigh accurately, your cakes and bread turn out better.
wichtigste: You weigh ingredients with kitchen scales.
They usually show the weight in grams.
The “Tare” button sets the display to zero.
The scales must stand on a level, firm surface.
Old scales with two pans are called balance scales.
For your own body weight you need bathroom scales.

abschnitte.text: Kitchen scales measure how heavy flour, sugar, butter or vegetables are. Most show the weight in **grams**; 1000 grams make one kilogram. Many household scales can weigh up to about 5 kilograms and are accurate to one gram. Some can also show millilitres for water or milk.

Older kitchen scales work with a **spring** that is squeezed by the weight and moves a pointer. Today's digital scales have a **load cell** with a piece of metal that bends very slightly under the load. Electronics measure this bending and convert it into grams. The number then appears on a display.

If you want to weigh flour in a bowl, the weight of the bowl gets in the way. So you put the empty bowl on the scales and press the **Tare** button. The display jumps to zero, and after that you only see the weight of the ingredient. If the bowl weighs 300 grams and the scales show 800 grams without tare, there are 500 grams of flour in it. Tare originally meant the weight of the packaging.

A recipe asks for 200 grams of sugar, for example. If 150 grams are already in the bowl, 50 grams are still missing. Accurate weighing is important in baking, because even small differences can change the dough. So that the scales measure correctly, they stand on a level, firm surface and not on a cloth.

As long as over 4000 years ago, people in ancient Egypt used **balance scales**. They have a beam with two pans. You put the goods in one pan and weights in the other until both hang at the same height. Later spring scales were added, and from the 1980s electronic scales became widespread.

With **bathroom scales** you measure your own body weight. Letter scales weigh post, and precision scales in pharmacies or laboratories measure to a thousandth of a gram. At the butcher's or in shops, scales must be officially checked. In Switzerland this is the job of the Federal Institute of Metrology, METAS.

begriffe.erklaerung: A unit of weight; 1000 grams make one kilogram.
The weight of the packaging or bowl, which is taken away from the display.
A part in digital scales that measures the weight electrically.
Scales with a beam and two pans, where you compare against weights.

gewusst: A litre of water weighs almost exactly one kilogram, so you can also weigh water instead of measuring it.
Scales actually measure the force with which an object presses down, and convert it into grams.
On the Moon, spring scales would show only about a sixth of the weight.

teile.einleitung: A line graph is a chart in which measurements are plotted as points and joined with a line. This lets you see at a glance how something changes over time. Temperature charts for fever, share price charts and temperature curves are well-known examples.
wichtigste: A line graph is especially good at showing a change over time.
Time is usually shown on the horizontal axis.
If the line rises, the values are increasing.
A horizontal line means that the values stay the same.
A steep line shows a fast change.
If the vertical axis does not start at 0, small differences look much bigger.
A line graph is ideal for the temperature over the course of a day.

abschnitte.text: A line graph has two **axes**: a horizontal one and a vertical one. The horizontal axis usually shows time, for example hours, months or years. The vertical axis shows the quantity measured, such as degrees Celsius or francs. For each measurement you plot a **data point** and join the points with a line. A good chart also has a title and labelled axes with units.

If the line rises from left to right, the values get bigger; if it falls, they get smaller. The steeper the line, the faster something is changing. A horizontal line means no change. If a graph shows 200 bike helmets sold in January and 260 in February, sales have risen by 60. The highest and lowest points of a line are called the **maximum** and **minimum**.

Weather reports use line graphs to show how warm it will get over a day or a week. Doctors draw temperature charts to see whether a fever is going down. In business, lines show how share prices develop. In a **climate graph**, the temperature is often shown as a line and the rainfall as bars. You can also draw several lines in the same graph, for example the temperatures of Zurich and Lugano for comparison.

Graphs can be misleading even when the numbers are not wrong. If the vertical axis does not start at 0, small differences suddenly look huge. A squashed or stretched **scale** also strongly changes the impression a curve gives. So whenever you read a graph, you should first look at the axes and their labels. Then you can tell whether a change really is dramatic.

The Scot **William Playfair** is considered the inventor of the line graph. In 1786 he published a book in which he showed England's trade with lines over the years. Before that, such figures were usually just listed in long tables. Today spreadsheet programs such as Excel create a line graph in a few clicks. Even so, children learn to draw graphs by hand at school so that they understand how they work.

begriffe.erklaerung: A line with a scale from which you read off the values.
A single measurement plotted on the graph.
The highest value in a series of data.
A chart that shows values as bars of different heights.

gewusst: Swiss weather services measure the temperature every ten minutes at many stations, which produces very accurate curves.
As well as the line graph, William Playfair also invented the bar chart and the pie chart.
A line graph is not good for things that have no order, for example the favourite colours of a class.

teile.einleitung: A live vaccine contains living but greatly weakened germs. They do not make you properly ill, but they teach the immune system to recognise and fight off the real germ. Well-known examples are the vaccinations against measles, mumps, rubella and chickenpox.
wichtigste: Live vaccines contain living, weakened germs.
The combined vaccination against measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) is a live vaccine.
There is also a live vaccine against chickenpox.
People with a severely weakened immune system are usually advised against live vaccines.
Traditionally, germs are weakened by passing them many times through cell cultures or other hosts.
In 1885 Louis Pasteur vaccinated the boy Joseph Meister against rabies.
In 1951 Max Theiler received the Nobel Prize for a live vaccine against yellow fever.
BCG protects young children from severe forms of tuberculosis.

abschnitte.text: A **vaccine** prepares the body for a disease without you having to go through it properly. In a **live vaccine**, the viruses or bacteria are still alive and can multiply a little in the body. But they are so greatly weakened that they cause mild symptoms at most. There are also inactivated vaccines, which contain only killed germs or parts of them.

The **immune system** recognises the weakened germs as foreign and makes defensive substances, the **antibodies**, as well as memory cells. If the real germ comes later, the body recognises it at once and can fight it quickly. Because the germs multiply a little, the protection is usually especially strong and long-lasting. So one or two doses are often enough.

Traditionally, the germs are grown many times in cell cultures or in other animals. This is called **passaging**. In the process the germs change so that they are hardly dangerous to humans any more. This is how, for example, the yellow fever vaccine 17D was made, for which Max Theiler received the Nobel Prize in 1951. Today researchers can also change germs on purpose in their genetic material.

In 1796 the English doctor Edward Jenner protected people from dangerous smallpox with harmless **cowpox**. The Frenchman Louis Pasteur developed weakened vaccines, and in 1885 he successfully vaccinated nine-year-old Joseph Meister against rabies. In 1921 the BCG vaccine against tuberculosis, named after Calmette and Guérin, was used for the first time in France. In the 1950s and 1960s Albert Sabin developed an oral polio vaccine with live viruses.

Live vaccines include the MMR vaccine against **measles**, mumps and rubella, as well as the vaccine against chickenpox. In Switzerland the MMR vaccine is recommended in two doses in early childhood. People are also vaccinated with a live vaccine against yellow fever, which occurs in tropical countries. For babies there is an oral vaccine against rotaviruses, which cause diarrhoea.

People with a severely weakened immune system should usually not receive live vaccines. In them, even the weakened germs could cause illness. These include, for example, people receiving chemotherapy for cancer. They are protected when as many people as possible around them are vaccinated, which is called **herd protection**. Families discuss with their doctor whether a vaccination is suitable.

begriffe.erklaerung: A substance that prepares the body for a disease.
A germ that has been changed so that it hardly makes you ill any more.
The body's defensive substances, which recognise and fight germs.
The body's defence system against germs.
Protection for unvaccinated people, because the disease can hardly spread when many people are vaccinated.

gewusst: The word vaccine comes from the Latin “vacca” for cow, because of Jenner's cowpox.
Thanks to worldwide vaccination, smallpox has officially been wiped out since 1980.
Joseph Meister later worked as a caretaker at the Pasteur Institute in Paris.

teile.einleitung: When growing crystals, you let crystals grow on purpose. This works even in the kitchen with sugar and water, but also in large factories. There, crystals are made for computer chips, watches and lasers.
wichtigste: Crystals have smooth faces and straight edges.
For sugar crystals you only need sugar and water.
More sugar dissolves in hot water than in cold water.
The crystals grow well on a thread or a wooden skewer.
The glass should stand still and not be shaken.
Beautiful crystals take several days.
Rock candy is made of large sugar crystals.
Natural rock crystals are found in the Swiss Alps.

abschnitte.text: A **crystal** is a solid substance in which the tiniest particles are arranged in a very regular way. You can imagine it like neatly stacked building blocks. That is why crystals have smooth faces, straight edges and often a typical shape. Table salt forms small cubes, snowflakes form six-pointed stars and quartz forms six-sided columns.

You dissolve as much sugar in hot water as will go in, because warm water can take up more sugar. Then you hang a thread or a wooden skewer in the glass. As the water cools and evaporates, it can no longer hold all the sugar. The sugar settles on the thread, and crystals grow. After several days to about two weeks, beautiful, large crystals form, as in **rock candy**.

A solution that contains more dissolved substance than it can really hold is called **supersaturated**. Crystals grow especially well from it. Keeping it still is important: if you shake the glass, you get many small crystals instead of a few large ones. A small starter crystal, the **seed crystal**, helps the growth. Similar experiments work with table salt, alum or copper sulphate, but copper sulphate is poisonous and should only be handled by adults.

In industry, huge and very pure crystals are grown. The most important example is **silicon**, from which computer chips and solar cells are made. In the Czochralski process, a crystal is slowly pulled upwards out of molten silicon. This produces rods that can be over a metre long. They are cut into wafer-thin slices.

As early as around 1900, the Frenchman Auguste Verneuil managed to make artificial rubies. Such synthetic rubies are still used today as jewel bearings in mechanical watches, including Swiss watches. In quartz watches, a small grown quartz crystal vibrates very evenly and keeps the beat. Sapphire glass for watch faces is also grown artificially.

In clefts in the Swiss Alps, **rock crystals**, which are clear quartz crystals, have been growing for millions of years. They formed from hot, mineral-rich water in the rock. People who search for crystals in the mountains are called **Strahler** in Switzerland. The Gotthard area and the Grimsel area are especially famous for crystal finds.

begriffe.erklaerung: A solid body with regularly arranged particles and smooth faces.
A liquid in which a substance such as sugar is spread out invisibly.
A solution that contains more dissolved substance than it can really hold.
A small starter crystal on which a larger crystal goes on growing.
A person who searches the Alps for rock crystals and other minerals.

gewusst: Almost every computer chip in the world comes from a grown silicon crystal.
People in the past thought rock crystal was frozen ice that never melts, which is where the Greek word krystallos for ice comes from.
Mechanical watches often contain about 20 to 30 tiny artificial rubies.

teile.einleitung: Food additives are substances added to food on purpose so that it keeps longer, looks better or has a particular texture. On packaging you can often recognise them by their E numbers. Many of them also occur in nature, for example in fruit or seaweed.
wichtigste: E numbers stand for permitted additives.
E 300 is ascorbic acid, which is vitamin C.
E 330 is citric acid.
An emulsifier such as lecithin joins fat and water.
Agar-agar is obtained from red seaweed.
Pectin from apples or citrus peel makes jam set.
Antioxidants stop fats from going rancid.
Preservatives such as sorbic acid slow down moulds and yeasts.

abschnitte.text: An **additive** is added to a food on purpose during production. It is meant, for example, to make it keep longer, to improve its colour or to give it a creamy texture. Salt, sugar or spices, on the other hand, count as normal ingredients. Every additive must be tested and approved before it can be used.

Approved additives have an **E number**; the E stands for Europe. The numbers are sorted into groups: E 100 to E 199 are mostly colourings, E 200 to E 299 preservatives and E 300 to E 399 mainly antioxidants and acidity regulators. From E 400 there are, among others, thickeners and gelling agents. Switzerland largely follows this system. The responsible authority is the Federal Food Safety and Veterinary Office, the FSVO.
