**E 300** is ascorbic acid, which is vitamin C; it protects fruit juices, for example, from turning brown. **E 330** is citric acid, which is found in lemons and gives many drinks a sour taste. E 322 is lecithin, which is often obtained from soya or sunflowers. These substances sound strange, but they are natural parts of many plants.

Fat and water do not normally mix, as you can see with oil in water. An **emulsifier** such as lecithin holds the two together, for example in chocolate, margarine or mayonnaise. **Pectin** comes from apples or citrus peel and makes jam set. Agar-agar is obtained from red seaweed and is a plant-based alternative to gelatine.

Food goes bad when moulds, yeasts or bacteria grow. **Preservatives** such as sorbic acid, E 200, slow down this growth, for example in bread, cheese or sauces. Antioxidants protect fats from the oxygen in the air so that they do not go rancid and smell bad. Cooling, drying or bottling also make food keep, without any additives at all.

All additives must be listed in the **list of ingredients** on the packaging, either by name or by E number. If you want to know what is in a food, you can look up the numbers. Approved substances are considered safe in the permitted amounts, but some people are sensitive to particular substances. Fresh, little-processed foods usually contain hardly any additives.

begriffe.erklaerung: A code for a food additive approved in Europe.
A substance that joins fat and water into an even mixture.
A substance that makes food keep longer by slowing down germs.
A substance that protects food from being changed by oxygen.
A substance that makes liquids firm and wobbly like jelly.

gewusst: Even vitamin C from oranges gets an E number as an additive, namely E 300.
Agar-agar gels so strongly that just a little powder can make a whole litre of liquid set.
Thousands of years ago people were already preserving meat and fish with salt and smoke.

teile.einleitung: Left-handedness means that a person is more skilful with the left hand than with the right. Left-handers prefer to write, draw, throw and cut with their left hand. About one in ten people in the world is left-handed.
wichtigste: A left-hander is someone who is more skilful with the left hand.
About 10 to 15 per cent of all people are left-handed.
Experts advise letting a left-handed child write with the left hand.
There are special scissors, fountain pens and other aids for left-handers.
International Left-Handers Day is on 13 August.
Someone who uses both hands equally well is ambidextrous.
There are also left-footed people, who are more skilful with the left foot.

abschnitte.text: Most people have one hand they prefer; this is called **handedness**. For left-handers this is the left hand, for right-handers the right. Handedness shows even in small children and can usually be clearly seen by nursery school age. Someone who uses both hands about equally well is called **ambidextrous**. In a similar way, there are people who prefer to kick a ball with their left foot, the left-footed.

abschnitte.titel: What the brain has to do with it
abschnitte.text: The brain consists of a left half and a right half. The nerves cross over, so the **right half of the brain** mainly controls the left side of the body. In left-handers, control of the hand is distributed differently from that in right-handers. Why someone becomes left-handed is not fully understood, but heredity plays a part. That is why some families have a striking number of left-handers.

In the past, the left hand was considered wrong in many countries, and children were forced at school to write with their right hand. This **forced switching** could lead to problems, for example difficulty concentrating or messy handwriting. Today we know that left-handedness is completely normal. Experts therefore advise letting children write with their stronger hand.

Many everyday objects are made for right-handers, such as scissors, tin openers or computer mice. For left-handers there are **left-handed scissors**, where the blades are the other way round so that you can see the cutting line. When writing in ink, the left hand passes over the fresh writing and can smudge it. Quick-drying ink, a special **left-handed fountain pen** and a sheet of paper placed at a slant help with this.

In some sports left-handers have an advantage, for example in tennis, fencing, table tennis or handball. Their opponents are mostly used to right-handers and have to adjust. The ball or the blade comes from an unfamiliar direction. That is why left-handers are often more common in top-level sport than in the rest of the population.

Since 1976, International Left-Handers Day has been celebrated every year on **13 August**. It is meant to draw attention to the fact that the world is often set up for right-handers. In many languages, words for right have a good meaning; in English, too, “right” also means correct. Today more and more schools and companies make sure that left-handers can manage well too.

begriffe.erklaerung: The preference for one hand that you use more skilfully.
Describes a person who can use both hands about equally well.
The former practice of forcing left-handers to write with their right hand.
Describes a person who is more skilful with the left foot.

gewusst: Some animals also have a favourite paw or favourite side, for example cats and parrots.
On left-handed scissors the blades are swapped, otherwise the upper blade would block the view of the cutting line.
The Latin word for left, sinister, also means ominous, which shows how left-handers used to be seen.

teile.einleitung: Short-term memory is the part of memory that holds information for only a short time. You use it, for example, to remember a phone number until you have typed it in. It is small and forgetful, but essential for thinking.
wichtigste: Without repetition, short-term memory holds information for only about 15 to 30 seconds.
According to George Miller, it can hold about seven items, plus or minus two.
In chunking, you group information into larger units.
Working memory holds information and works on it at the same time, for example in mental arithmetic.
The hippocampus is important for getting content into long-term memory.
After brain surgery in 1953, Henry Molaison could no longer permanently remember new experiences.
Spaced repetition helps most to keep what you have learned for a long time.

abschnitte.text: Memory works in several stages. First, sense impressions land in the sensory store for fractions of a second. What we pay attention to goes into **short-term memory**, where it disappears again after about 15 to 30 seconds unless it is repeated. Only part of it reaches **long-term memory**, where it can stay for years. The researchers Richard Atkinson and Richard Shiffrin described this stage model in 1968.

In 1956 the American psychologist **George Miller** found that people can hold about seven items at once, plus or minus two. These can be digits, letters or words. More recent research suggests that it is often only about four items. That is why a long row of numbers is so easily forgotten.

You can remember more if you group information into packages. This is called **chunking**, from the English word “chunk”. The digits 1, 2, 9, 1 are easier to remember as the year 1291, the year the Swiss Confederation was founded. That is also why phone numbers are written in groups. A chess expert can remember whole positions because he sees them as familiar patterns.

In mental arithmetic you have to hold numbers in your head and calculate with them at the same time. This combination is called **working memory**. The British researchers Alan Baddeley and Graham Hitch described it in more detail in 1974. It has one part for language and sounds and one for pictures and places. You also need it when reading a long sentence, so as not to forget the beginning.

In 1953 the American **Henry Molaison** had brain surgery because of severe epileptic seizures. The doctors also removed large parts of both **hippocampi**. After that he could no longer permanently remember new experiences, even though his short-term memory worked. He became famous under the initials H. M., and through him it was discovered that short-term and long-term memory are separate systems.

When someone reads a list to you, you often remember the last words well, because they are still in your short-term memory. The first words also often stick, because you have repeated them more often. To keep knowledge for a long time, **spaced repetition** helps, which means learning several times with gaps of days in between. Testing yourself, for example with flashcards or quiz questions, works better than just reading again. Getting enough sleep also helps, because the brain strengthens what you have learned while you sleep.

begriffe.erklaerung: A store that holds a small amount of information for seconds.
A store in which knowledge and memories can stay for years.
Grouping single items into larger, meaningful packages.
The part of memory that holds information and works on it at the same time.
An area of the brain that helps to store new memories permanently.

gewusst: The hippocampus is called that because its shape is reminiscent of a seahorse, hippokampos in Greek.

teile.einleitung: A fridge is a household appliance that keeps food cool so that it stays fresh for longer. It does not make cold but pumps heat from the inside to the outside. Today there is a fridge in almost every kitchen in Switzerland.
wichtigste: Germs grow more slowly in the fridge, so food stays fresh for longer.
A temperature of about 5 degrees Celsius is recommended.
The compressor squeezes the gaseous refrigerant.

Carl von Linde built an important refrigerating machine around 1876.
With the fridge door open, the kitchen gets warmer overall, not cooler.

abschnitte.text: In the cold, **germs** such as bacteria and moulds multiply much more slowly. That is why milk, meat, cheese and vegetables stay fresh for longer in the fridge. For the household fridge, a temperature of about 5 degrees Celsius is recommended. In the **freezer** it is much colder, usually about minus 18 degrees, so that ice cream stays hard.

Inside the fridge, a **refrigerant** flows round a closed circuit of pipes. Inside the fridge it evaporates and takes up heat as it does so, much as sweat cools the skin when it evaporates. The **compressor** sucks in the gas and squeezes it, which makes it hot. In the grid at the back it gives off its heat to the kitchen and becomes liquid again, then the cycle starts all over.

It is not equally cold everywhere in the fridge. The **vegetable drawer** is usually right at the bottom; it is a little damper and less cold there. Meat and fish belong on the coldest shelf, usually just above the vegetable drawer. Hot food, such as a pan of freshly cooked soup, should first be left to cool before you put it in.

In the past, food was kept in a cool **cellar** or put in ice boxes filled with blocks of ice. In winter people sawed ice out of lakes for this and stored it in ice houses. The German engineer **Carl von Linde** built an important refrigerating machine around 1876, which was first used in breweries. Electric fridges for households spread from the 1920s in America and later in Europe too.

Fridges used to contain refrigerants that damaged the protective **ozone layer**; today more environmentally friendly substances are used. If you leave the door open for a long time, cold air escapes and the fridge uses more electricity. You also cannot cool a kitchen with the door open, because the fridge gives off more heat at the back than the cold it lets out at the front. The energy label shows when you buy one how economical an appliance is.

teile.einleitung: A pie chart is a round diagram that shows how a whole is divided into parts. Each part is a slice of the pie, and the bigger the share, the bigger the slice. That is why it is called a pie chart.
wichtigste: A pie chart shows shares of a whole.
A whole circle has 360 degrees.
All the parts together make 100 per cent.
A share of 25 per cent corresponds to an angle of 90 degrees.
A share of 10 per cent corresponds to 36 degrees.
An angle of 120 degrees corresponds to one third.
In everyday language it is also called a cake chart in German.

abschnitte.text: A pie chart is a circle divided into several **sectors**. Each sector stands for a part of the whole, for example a party in an election or a flavour of ice cream. The sectors are usually drawn in different colours and labelled with a **key**. Together all the parts always make 100 per cent.

abschnitte.titel: How to work out the angles
abschnitte.text: A full circle has 360 degrees, and that corresponds to 100 per cent. So one per cent corresponds to 3.6 degrees. For 25 per cent you multiply 25 by 3.6 and get 90 degrees, a right angle. For 10 per cent it is 36 degrees. A sector of 120 degrees is one third of the circle, because 360 divided by 3 is 120.

In a class of 30 children, 6 come to school by bike. That is one fifth of the class, so 20 per cent. The angle for it is 360 divided by 30, times 6, which is 72 degrees. Using a **set square** or a protractor, you then draw the sector from the centre.

Pie charts are especially good for showing **shares**, for example how pocket money is divided up. They work best with only a few parts, about two to six. With many small slices it becomes confusing, and slices of similar size are hard to compare. For changes over time a line graph is better, and for comparisons a **bar chart**.

The Scottish engineer **William Playfair** is considered the inventor of the pie chart. He published one of the first pie charts in 1801. Playfair also invented the bar chart and the line graph. Later the nurse Florence Nightingale also became famous for using a kind of pie chart to show what soldiers died of in the Crimean War.

Pie charts can be found in newspapers, school books and presentations. After votes and elections in Switzerland, for example, they show how the seats are shared out or the share of yes votes. With spreadsheet programs on a computer they can be made in a few seconds. A version with a hole in the middle is called a **doughnut chart**.
